planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Honshu is a single-flowered selection prized for the largest blooms of any kerria cultivar.

directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Honshu is a vigorous single-flowered kerria selection distinguished by its unusually large, two-inch, golden-yellow blooms with broad, overlapping petals that open earlier in spring and continue longer than the species type, set against bright green, arching, bamboo-like canes. Like other kerria it tolerates considerably more shade than most flowering shrubs, often coloring best and blooming most heavily in partial or even full shade rather than hot sun. It suckers to form a colony over time; thin out a portion of the oldest canes at ground level right after flowering each year to maintain an open, well-lit habit that shows off the large flowers.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Chiba Gold is a gold-leaved sport that bleaches and scorches if given more than early morning direct sun.

directions: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Chiba Gold is grown chiefly for its foliage, which emerges chartreuse-gold in spring, fades to a creamy, white-flecked lime green through summer, and turns clear yellow in fall, on the same bright green, arching, bamboo-like canes typical of the species; single golden-yellow flowers open in mid-spring but are secondary to the long season of foliage color. Because the gold leaf pigment bleaches and scorches in strong sun, site this cultivar where it receives only early morning light or dappled shade for the rest of the day, a niche few other variegated shrubs can fill. It suckers moderately to form a colony over time; prune out a portion of the oldest canes at ground level right after flowering each year to keep new, brightly colored growth coming.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs
